content: Fibrous proteins, also known as scleroproteins, are elongated, filamentous protein molecules that belong to one of the two primary classes of tertiary structure proteins, the other being globular proteins. These proteins are exclusively found in animals. They adopt a rod-like or wire-like shape and typically serve as inert structural or storage proteins. Fibrous proteins are generally insoluble in water. This insolubility arises from the presence of hydrophobic R-groups that protrude from the protein molecule, causing them to aggregate. The amino acid sequences that make up fibrous proteins often consist of repetitive residues, such as those found in the collagen triple helix. Their structures frequently include cross-links between chains, such as disulfide bonds (Cys-Cys bonds) that occur between keratin chains. Compared to fibrous proteins, globular proteins are more prone to denaturation. Fibrous proteins primarily function in the construction of connective tissues, tendons, bone matrix, and muscle fibers. Examples of fibrous proteins include keratins, collagens, and elastins.
